newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Dostum blasts Pakistan for meddling in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Dostum blasts Pakistan for meddling in Afghanistan.

text.p: A spokesman for northern Afghan militia leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum attacked Pakistan on Monday for what he called interference in Afghan affairs in support of the Islamic Taleban movement.

The spokesman, General Yousif, who uses only one name, told reporters that the Supreme Defence Council alliance of factions hostile to the Taleban believed that the Islamic radicals who seized Kabul a month ago were dancing to Islamabad's tune.
"The Taleban have no independent intentions," he said. "The position of the Supreme Defence Council is that the Taleban are acting under pressure from abroad.
"The prisoners and documents we have are signs of direct interference by Pakistan in Afghanistan's internal affairs," Yousif said without giving details of the evidence.
Pakistan has long denied charges that it supports the Taleban, saying it favours no Afghan faction over another.
Ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood has often made such accusations in the past, but Dostum has not previously let his spokesmen publicly criticise Pakistan.
Pakistan said on Sunday it would not attend a regional conference called hastily by Iran for Tuesday, citing problems with the agenda and guest list, which includes arch-rival India.

"Pakistan had already maintained that only those countries which were directly concerned with the welfare of Afghanistan should attend any conference of neighbouring or regional countries, and such a conference should follow rather than precede an intra-Afghan dialogue," the Foreign Ministry said.

United Nations special envoy Norbert Holl, who has been trying to broker a ceasefire between the Taleban and its foes, sent a representative, Francis Okelo, to Tehran on Monday to attend the conference, said a U.N. official in Islamabad.
Yousif spoke pessimistically of the prospects for a truce with the Taleban, now defending Kabul against what has become a joint assault by the forces of former rivals Dostum and Masood.

"If the Taleban really wanted a peaceful solution they would send their own people. First they sent (Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah) Babar, then Holl, but not their own people," he said, but added that the anti-Taleban alliance would not close the door for negotiations.
There has been no apparent progress in the ceasefire efforts while battles north of Kabul, in which both sides have used air power, have intensified in the last few days.
The U.N. official said Holl, a German diplomat, was committed to his peace mission. "Don't worry, he is not at all disillusioned," the official said. "He is still very fresh."
The Taleban movement was born in religious schools in Pakistan two years ago. The militia's capture of Kabul gave it control of some three-quarters of Afghanistan.
